summary: Defines the Network Control Protocol for establishing and configuring remote bridging over PPP links. It is on the standards track and was replaced by RFC 3518.

plainLanguage.summary: Two networks can be joined across a long cable as if they were one. This is how two ends of a PPP link agree to do that.

questions: how to bridge lans over ppp
subtitle: How to connect remote Local Area Networks over point-to-point links

tldr.problem: Organizations need to bridge separate Local Area Networks across long-distance connections like leased lines, but different bridging methods (transparent bridging for Ethernet, source routing for Token Ring) exist, and they need clear rules for doing this over PPP links.
tldr.mechanism: The Bridging Control Protocol (BCP) is a network control protocol that negotiates bridging parameters between two systems, carries LAN frames across a PPP link while preserving checksums and handling VLANs, and supports all major bridging methods. BCP configuration options let systems agree on bridge identification, MAC types, and features like frame compression.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2878 was replaced by RFC 3518, which updated it with better VLAN support and simplified the protocol. Remote bridging over PPP became standard practice for connecting distant LANs before VPN technology became prevalent.

facts.label: Frame Header Size
facts.value: Variable; 1 to 2 bytes for flags and padding count, then MAC type and frame

facts.label: Configuration Options
facts.value: 8 types for bridging parameters, MAC types, and VLAN support

facts.label: VLAN Support
facts.value: IEEE 802.1Q VLAN tags (priority 3 bits, canonical flag, VLAN ID 12 bits)

today: RFC 2878 was obsoleted by RFC 3518, which incorporated IEEE 802.1D-1998 and 802.1Q standards for better VLAN support and refined the protocol based on deployment experience. Remote bridging over PPP has been largely superseded by VPN and modern layer 3 routing, but the protocol remains in use in legacy networks and is part of the historical foundation of bridging standards.

sections.title: Bridging Basics
sections.content:
Bridging is a layer 2 (data link layer) technique that connects multiple LANs so they work like one big network. Stations on different LANs can talk to each other without knowing they are separated.

The RFC defines three main bridging approaches: Transparent Bridging (learns MAC addresses by watching traffic and forwards based on a table, used by Ethernet and IEEE 802 standards), Source Routing (the sending station includes the path in the packet, used by Token Ring and FDDI), and SR-TB Translational Bridging (bridges between transparent and source-routed networks). Remote bridges connect LANs via a long line, such as a leased T1 or using PPP.

Redundant paths create loops that confuse bridging, so the Spanning Tree Protocol detects them and blocks some connections to eliminate loops. In switched LAN environments, Virtual LANs (VLANs) partition a single bridge into separate communities so traffic from one VLAN does not reach another.
sections.plainLanguage: Transparent bridging is like having a librarian who watches what books people ask for, remembers where each person sits, and forwards requests to the right desk. Source routing is like putting the directions on the request itself. Remote bridging does this over a long cable.

sections.title: BCP Protocol Design
sections.content:
The Bridging Control Protocol is a specific instance of the PPP Link Control Protocol (LCP). It runs after PPP has established the link and reached the Network Layer Protocol phase, and it negotiates the parameters for how the two bridging systems will work together.

BCP defines eight configuration options: Bridge-Identification (tells the other end this system's bridge number for source-route bridges), Line-Identification (the LAN segment number of the line), MAC-Support (which frame types this system can handle, such as Ethernet or FDDI), Tinygram-Compression (to shrink small padded frames), LAN-Identification (now obsolete), MAC-Address (specifies a MAC address), Spanning Tree Protocol (carries old BPDU format for backward compatibility), and IEEE-802-Tagged-Frame (allows VLAN tags). Systems also carry Bridge Protocol Data Units (BPDUs) used by Spanning Tree and GARP protocols for managing the network topology and multicast groups.

BCP respects the independence of the bridging systems: either system can choose to disable spanning tree on the link by not exchanging BPDUs, which is useful if network administrators want to run separate spanning trees in each region.
sections.plainLanguage: Before the two systems start sending office network packets, they exchange a few messages to agree on ground rules: which machine types they support, whether to compress tiny packets, and how to handle special management frames.

sections.title: Frame Format on the Line
sections.content:
LAN frames arriving at a bridge get wrapped with extra PPP headers before crossing the WAN line. The frame format includes a flag byte (F for FCS present, Z for padding needed), the MAC type (which of the six defined LAN types), and then the original LAN frame and optionally its checksum. The design preserves the original LAN Frame Check Sequence (FCS) from the sending station so the receiving end can verify the frame has not been corrupted. If a frame had no FCS originally, the packet is explicitly tagged so the receiver knows to calculate one before putting it on the receiving LAN.

For systems that bridge multiple frame types, the RFC specifies different layouts for Ethernet (802.3) and Token Ring/FDDI (802.5, 802.4, FDDI). Each format includes the Destination MAC Address, Source MAC Address, and the link-layer data, optionally followed by padding. When VLAN tagging is in use (IEEE 802.1Q), the PPP frame also includes a priority field (3 bits) and the VLAN ID (12 bits) so virtual communities stay isolated across the link.

Tinygram compression saves bandwidth on slow links by stripping trailing zeros from small frames and compressing them; the receiving end pads them back to the minimum LAN frame size before forwarding.
sections.plainLanguage: A LAN frame is like a postcard. BCP puts it in an envelope (the PPP wrapper) with a label (MAC type) and sometimes marks special things like the return address and whether the handwriting got smudged.

sections.title: Configuration and Management
sections.content:
Before bridging traffic flows, the two systems exchange configuration options using PPP's Configure-Request, Configure-Ack, Configure-Nak, and Configure-Reject messages. Each option has a Type, Length, and value.

The Bridge-Identification option is used only in source-route bridging when the two systems model themselves as two halves of a single bridge. Each system announces its bridge number and LAN segment number. If the numbers do not match, the systems can either declare an error or the higher-numbered system adopts the lower number to avoid misconfiguration. The Line-Identification option works the same way but is used when each system is modeled as an independent bridge with its own bridge number, and the line itself is treated as a virtual LAN segment.

The MAC-Support option lets implementations announce which frame types (Ethernet, Token Ring, FDDI) they support, which helps the peer system avoid sending unsupported types. Implementations support canonical and non-canonical address formats: the RFC requires implementations to support lower-numbered variants if they support higher ones, for backward compatibility.

Management of bridge protocols (Spanning Tree, GVRP for VLAN registration, GMRP for multicast filtering) occurs through special destination MAC addresses. Frames destined for 01-80-c2-00-00-00 (Bridge Group Address) carry Spanning Tree BPDUs. Frames for 01-80-c2-00-00-21 carry GVRP data to manage VLAN membership dynamically. The RFC also specifies how old-format BPDUs from RFC 1638 bridges are handled for backward compatibility.
sections.plainLanguage: During setup, the two machines check off a list: what frame types can you handle? Do you want me to squeeze tiny packets? Which virtual communities should I support? This negotiation ensures both sides speak the same language.

sections.title: Security and Deployment Constraints
sections.content:
RFC 2878 notes that the protocol itself provides no authentication or confidentiality. All authentication must rely on the underlying PPP authentication mechanisms (CHAP, PAP, or others). The protocol also does not prevent resource exhaustion attacks: a malicious or misconfigured system can flood the link with frames, consuming bandwidth. Network administrators must rely on physical link protection and careful configuration.

Maximum Receive Unit (MRU) negotiation is critical: because MAC frames (such as Ethernet with its full headers) are larger than the default PPP MRU of 1500 octets, systems MUST negotiate a larger MRU or fragmentation will occur and bridging will fail. The RFC recommends that implementations support loopback detection and link-quality monitoring using PPP's Magic Number mechanism, so broken links are detected quickly.

The RFC does not specify what happens when a bridge is bridging more than two communities across a single link: packet ordering is critical for some protocols. The RFC recommends either forcing single-threaded operation or using PPP Multilink to bind multiple physical lines into one logical link while preserving order.
sections.plainLanguage: This protocol assumes the cable connecting the two buildings is secure and that the right people are on both ends. If someone sends a flood of junk traffic, the cable can get clogged. The two systems should check that the cable is working and agree on how fast they will talk.
